title: ARIA’s mission: high-risk science, real-world impact
label: 8 September 2026 · ARIA overview and scrutiny
summary: Dr Kathleen Fisher, ARIA’s CEO, explains how the agency picks high-risk, high-reward science projects, manages and measures them, and tries to turn breakthroughs into practical benefits for the UK—while discussing intellectual property, regional spread of funding, links with other funders, governance concerns and lessons from DARPA.

speakers.label: Dr Kathleen Fisher
speakers.name: Dr Kathleen Fisher
speakers.role: Chief Executive Officer, Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA)

chapters.title: What ARIA is trying to do
chapters.takeaway: ARIA backs very risky, ambitious science and measures success by breakthroughs, real-world impact, and changing how people think.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Dr Fisher. You became ARIA CEO in February. Tell us briefly your top priorities and how you’ll steer ARIA as it grows.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Thanks. ARIA is meant to fund high‑risk, high‑reward projects — the sort of work that could change whole fields. My priorities are getting ARIA to steady state: hiring programme leaders, running programmes well and translating discoveries into benefits for people and the economy.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We judge success three ways: big scientific breakthroughs, real societal or economic impact, and shifting mindset — getting people excited about shaping the future rather than just reacting to it.

chapters.title: Concrete projects and how they work
chapters.takeaway: ARIA funds focused programmes that combine science teams, engineering partners and outside help to remove barriers and speed progress.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can you give a few programmes that show how ARIA works in practice?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Sure. Forecasting tipping points is one. It looks for early warnings of big climate shifts, for example changes in the Atlantic ocean currents or Greenland ice melt.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: One creator company, Oshen in Plymouth, builds small solar/wind-powered sea robots — ‘sea stars’ — to gather ocean data cheaply instead of using expensive ships. They’ve gone from one to five robots and plan fifty in a year.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Those robots even rode out Hurricane Humberto and returned useful data. That’s an example of progress even if the programme’s ultimate 'North Star' goal still takes time.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Another example: activation partners. These are companies ARIA contracts to provide routine specialised help — like bespoke engineering — so scientists don’t spend months finding and paying for engineers.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Amod0 Design in Sheffield built batteries that operate at −50°C in just three months, a job that could’ve taken a year and a half through normal grant routes. That benefits multiple projects at once.

chapters.title: How ARIA manages and judges projects
chapters.takeaway: Programmes set goals and milestones, get frequent director oversight, outside expert review, and can pivot or stop quickly if things aren’t working.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: How do you track progress across so many different, risky projects? Three years can feel short for real research.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We set programme-specific milestones up front. Programme directors meet creators quarterly, use simple red/amber/green checks, and report annually with outside scientific and translation reviewers.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Crucially, funding stops by default. If a project looks promising we deliberately decide to extend or add resources; if not, we terminate. That avoids automatic roll‑on funding.

turns.speaker: Lord Duncan of Springbank
turns.text: If a project can’t reach its original goal but produces useful work, can you re‑direct it?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes. Programme directors constantly discuss pivots with teams. We’re also writing contracts to be more flexible so pivots don’t mean slow, costly redrafts.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: What do you look for in programme directors, since they carry a lot of discretion?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We want people with technical depth, cross-discipline breadth, judgement, entrepreneurial drive, communication and leadership. They must learn fast and accept feedback — they’re term‑limited, so speed matters.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We hire directors in cohorts so we get balance — academics and people from industry — and they support each other as a class.

chapters.title: Translation, UK benefit and intellectual property
chapters.takeaway: ARIA focuses on turning science into social and economic value, prefers creators to keep IP to ease company formation, and works to keep value in the UK while prioritising getting innovations to market.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: ARIA must bring economic benefit specifically to the UK. How do you ensure discoveries and companies stay and create UK jobs and wealth?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We prioritise crossing the 'valley of death' — getting tech from lab to real users. We hired a chief translation officer to plan market routes, work with entrepreneurs and coordinate government where useful.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We generally let creators keep intellectual property (IP). That makes it easier for them to form companies and attract investors quickly, which improves survival chances — and most creators are UK‑based.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: But should ARIA prefer UK investors so the value stays here?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We want companies to stay in the UK. If UK investors step up great; if not, a capable foreign investor who keeps the company in the UK is better than the company failing or leaving. We require some protections and royalties if IP is sold abroad.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Are you reviewing ARIA’s IP rules?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We constantly review policy. Our current view is that creator‑owned IP best helps translation and UK benefit, but we’ll change if we find a better approach.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: Could government procurement be used to help companies scale and stay in the UK?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes. We’re already exploring advanced market commitments and partnerships where a government pledge to buy or pilot tech creates a market and helps crossing the valley of death.

chapters.title: Geography, other funders and governance
chapters.takeaway: ARIA is trying to spread opportunities across the UK, coordinates with other funders to avoid wasteful duplication, and accepts the need for clear conflict-of-interest rules.

turns.speaker: Lord Booth
turns.text: Most ARIA money has gone to the 'golden triangle' — London, Oxford, Cambridge. What are you doing about regional spread?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We require programme directors to do a UK-wide discovery process, talk to researchers in every region, and justify who they’ve reached. We’re working with regional science contacts in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We’re also improving how we collect data: right now we track prime contracts, but subcontractors spread the money further. Better data will show whether the gap is applicants or awards.

turns.speaker: Baroness Jones of Whitchurch
turns.text: Talking is fine but the money statistics haven’t changed. Will you make concrete changes to fund more outside the south‑east?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I hear that. The discovery work and outreach — Newcastle, Sheffield, Plymouth, Belfast — aim to find talent outside the golden triangle. We’re refining outreach and simplifying application routes where possible.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: How do you avoid overlapping other foundations' work? Workshops are often filled with people with vested interests.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We use a mix of discovery workshops and AI tools to read literature and spot overlap. External reviewers — who can’t get funded on that programme — check distinctiveness. If overlap appears, we talk to other funders and adjust.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: On the recent chair appointment controversy, ARIA didn’t pick the chair. But did the executive raise concerns about conflicts of interest?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The appointment and mitigations were decisions by the oversight body (BIST). ARIA wasn’t part of that decision. But I did get feedback from the sector that people were worried, and I agree a chair must not have conflicts that impede ARIA.

chapters.title: ARIA compared to DARPA and final aims
chapters.takeaway: ARIA borrows DARPA’s approach — director-driven, bold goals, quick pivots — but is smaller, civilian-focused and must prove its success; Dr Fisher’s aim is tangible breakthroughs and a healthy, sustainable agency.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: You’ve worked at DARPA. How similar are the agencies and what lessons does ARIA take?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Both fund daring, director-led projects and expect failure. DARPA is larger, often works on classified defence needs and has an established customer base. ARIA is civilian, smaller and must show early results to prove its model here.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We’re learning DARPA’s best practices: flexible contracts, phased funding, technical evaluation teams and active programme management. We’ll adapt those to the UK context.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, what will you most like to look back on in a few years?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Delivering real breakthroughs that matter — science that changes practice and improves lives. Also, getting ARIA to steady state with programmes ending and starting at a good rhythm, and keeping it a place where talented people can make big, positive change.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: An example: a programme exploring the innate immune system could lead to a broad antiviral treatment lasting months — high risk, but huge potential public-health and economic benefit.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Dr Fisher. We appreciate the clarity and will follow progress closely.

glossary.definition: The UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency, a government body that funds high‑risk, high‑reward science and technology projects.
The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, a government agency that funds high‑risk research, often for defence applications.
The oversight body mentioned in the session that made the chair appointment decisions for ARIA.
An ARIA-funded lead researcher or team responsible for running a project and often forming companies to develop results.
Staff who design and run ARIA programmes, choose and monitor projects, and decide on funding actions.
Main contracts awarded directly by the funder to a company or organisation to deliver work or services.
Companies or individuals hired by the prime contractor to carry out parts of the contracted work.
A simple traffic‑light system used to indicate project status or levels of risk and priority (red=problem, green=good).
